title: Noah Buckley - Political Scientist
text:
Assistant Professor of Political Science


Department of Political Science, Trinity College Dublin


Email · Google Scholar · SSRN
I am an assistant professor (with tenure) in the Department of Political Science at Trinity College Dublin. I received my Ph.D. from Columbia University in 2016 and was previously a postdoctoral associate at NYU Abu Dhabi.
My research focuses on authoritarian politics in Putin-era Russia: how autocratic regimes sustain themselves, how the mass public understands their authoritarian environment, and why corruption persists. I use quantitative methods and original micro-level data, including the largest individual-level database of Russian public opinion survey responses.
My work has appeared in the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, Comparative Political Studies, Comparative Politics, Journal of Experimental Political Science, Europe-Asia Studies, and Post-Soviet Affairs.
(Looking for Noah M. Buckley-Farlee? That’s me.)

title: Research
text:
The Demand for Elections under Autocracy: Regime Approval and the Elimination of Local Elections in Russia (with Quintin Beazer and Ora John Reuter) American Journal of Political Science, 2024


Abstract

Why do some authoritarian regimes hold elections while others do not? We argue that regime approval shapes the decision to cancel elections.


Endogenous Popularity: How Perceptions of Regime Support Affect the Popularity of Authoritarian Regimes (with Kyle Marquardt, Ora John Reuter, and Ekaterina Tertytchnaya) American Political Science Review, 2024, 118(2):1046-1052 DOI


Abstract

Do perceptions of a regime’s popularity affect actual support for it? Using survey experiments in Russia, we show that information about the regime’s popularity causally increases support for it.


Staying Out of Trouble: Criminal Cases Against Russian Mayors (with Ora John Reuter, Michael Rochlitz, and Anton Aisin) Comparative Political Studies, 2022, 55(9):1539-1568


Abstract

Why are some local officials prosecuted while others are not? We examine criminal cases against Russian mayors.


Who Reports Crime? Citizen Engagement with the Police in Russia and Georgia (with Timothy Frye, Scott Gehlbach, and Lauren McCarthy) Europe-Asia Studies, 2021, 73(1):8-35

Performance Incentives under Autocracy: Evidence from Russia’s Regions (with Ora John Reuter) Comparative Politics, 2019, 51(2):239-266


Abstract

We find that performance-based appointments are more frequent in less competitive regions. In more competitive regions, the political imperatives of maintaining a political machine may lead regime leaders to abandon cadre policies that promote economic development.


Staring at the West through Kremlin-tinted Glasses: Russian Mass and Elite Divergence in Attitudes toward the United States, European Union, and Ukraine before and after Crimea (with Joshua A. Tucker) Post-Soviet Affairs, 2019, 35(5-6):365-375

Local Elections in Authoritarian Regimes: An Elite-Based Theory with Evidence from Russian Mayoral Elections (with Ora John Reuter, Guzel Garifullina, and Alexandra Shubenkova) Comparative Political Studies, 2016, 49(5)


Abstract

We argue that autocrats use subnational elections to co-opt and assuage powerful subnational elites. When subnational elites control significant political resources, leaders may need to co-opt them in order to govern cost-effectively.


Cooperating with the State: Evidence from Survey Experiments on Policing (with Timothy Frye, Scott Gehlbach, and Lauren McCarthy) Journal of Experimental Political Science, 2016, 3(2):124-139

The Political Economy of Russian Gubernatorial Elections and Appointments (with Timothy Frye, Guzel Garifullina, and Ora John Reuter) Europe-Asia Studies, 2014, 66(8)

Elections, Appointments, and Human Capital: The Case of Russian Mayors (with Guzel Garifullina, Ora John Reuter, and Alexandra Shubenkova) Demokratizatsiya, 2014, 22(1)

title: Website Updates (Feb 2026)
text:
Wider sidebar: Increased from ~200px to 260px for better prominence
Better centering: Added 80px left margin to content area for improved balance
Responsive: Layout adjusts appropriately on mobile devices





Added comprehensive meta descriptions to all pages
Configured Open Graph and Twitter Card tags for social sharing
Added structured keywords for search engines
Enabled sitemap generation
Added site-url configuration for proper indexing
Set up Google Analytics placeholder (update with your GA4 ID)





Created markdown-based CV in ../cv/ directory
Supports multiple output formats:

HTML (for web viewing)
PDF (for download, matches current CV style)
LaTeX (can export if needed)

Build script (cv/build_cv.sh) generates all formats
Easy to maintain - edit one markdown file, get all formats





From the website/ directory:
quarto render
This will regenerate all HTML files in the docs/ folder.



From the cv/ directory:
./build_cv.sh
This creates HTML and PDF versions of the CV.



The site is configured for GitHub Pages. After making changes:
cd website/
quarto render
cd docs/
git add .
git commit -m "Update website"
git push



To create a page that’s not in the sidebar menu:

Create a .qmd file in the website directory (e.g., hidden-page.qmd)
Don’t add it to _quarto.yml sidebar contents
The page will be accessible at /hidden-page.html but won’t appear in navigation

To make it truly hidden from search engines, add to the page YAML:
---
title: "Hidden Page"
robots: noindex, nofollow
---



To enable analytics: 1. Get your Google Analytics 4 (GA4) measurement ID 2. In _quarto.yml, replace "G-XXXXXXXXXX" with your actual ID



A sitemap is automatically generated at docs/sitemap.xml when you render the site. Submit this to: - Google Search Console - Bing Webmaster Tools




Build and preview the updated site
If satisfied, commit and push changes
Set up Google Analytics (optional)
Submit sitemap to search engines
Consider adding a robots.txt file if needed
